videos.title: Endocrine system overview
videos.purpose: Identify how hormone transport differs from a neural pathway.
videos.fallback: Hormones enter blood and affect cells with suitable receptors. A hormone reaching a tissue does not guarantee a response.

videos.title: Thyroid regulation
videos.purpose: Name the three glands or regions and the feedback signal.
videos.fallback: The hypothalamus stimulates the anterior pituitary, which releases TSH. Thyroid hormone feeds back to reduce upstream stimulation.

videos.title: Blood glucose regulation
videos.purpose: Explain why insulin and glucagon are an antagonistic pair.
videos.fallback: Insulin promotes glucose uptake and storage. Glucagon stimulates the liver to release glucose when blood glucose is low.

videos.title: Diabetes and insulin
videos.purpose: Distinguish inadequate insulin production from a reduced response to insulin.
videos.fallback: Type 1 involves loss of insulin-producing beta cells. Type 2 involves insulin resistance and may also involve insufficient insulin production. These are simplified learning models, not diagnoses.

videos.title: Adrenal hormone pathways
videos.purpose: Identify which pathway uses sympathetic neurons and which uses ACTH.
videos.fallback: Sympathetic stimulation reaches the adrenal medulla directly. The hypothalamus–pituitary pathway uses ACTH to stimulate adrenal cortisol secretion.

videos.title: The cortisol pathway
videos.purpose: Follow the cortisol pathway and identify where feedback acts.
videos.fallback: CRH stimulates ACTH release; ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex; cortisol feeds back on the hypothalamus and pituitary.

videos.title: Short-term and continuing stress responses
videos.purpose: Distinguish a useful response from a claim about prolonged exposure.
videos.fallback: Cortisol supports fuel availability and has anti-inflammatory effects. A prolonged pattern is not equivalent to a brief stress response.

videos.title: Connecting endocrine responses
videos.purpose: For each example, name the trigger, hormone, target and effect.
videos.fallback: A complete explanation connects a change in an internal variable with a gland, messenger, responding tissue and feedback effect.

videos.title: Hormone production, release and targets
videos.purpose: Check that production, storage and release are not treated as the same action.
videos.fallback: ADH is produced in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. The kidneys are its target, not its source.

videos.title: Reconstructing hormone pathways
videos.purpose: Pause to sketch the regulation pathway before checking the lesson.
videos.fallback: Review gland–hormone–target relationships, then explain how the response changes the original stimulus.

videos.title: Comparing antagonistic hormones
videos.purpose: Compare hormone pairs by their effects on a named variable.
videos.fallback: Insulin and glucagon act in opposite directions on blood glucose. PTH and calcitonin have contrasting effects on blood calcium.

videos.title: Adrenal cortex and medulla
videos.purpose: Distinguish the adrenal cortex from the adrenal medulla.
videos.fallback: The medulla releases epinephrine and norepinephrine; the cortex produces cortisol and aldosterone. Their control pathways differ.

videos.title: Predicting feedback changes
videos.purpose: Predict what changes downstream when one part of a feedback loop fails.
videos.fallback: Start with the stated defect and follow its consequences. High TSH with low thyroxine is consistent with a thyroid response problem when upstream control is intact.

videos.title: Male reproductive anatomy
videos.purpose: Follow the production, maturation and transport sites.
videos.fallback: Sperm form in seminiferous tubules, mature in the epididymis and move through the vas deferens, ejaculatory duct and urethra. Accessory glands add fluid to semen.

videos.title: Sperm development
videos.purpose: Distinguish the reproductive-cell stages from their supporting cells.
videos.fallback: A primary spermatocyte completes two meiotic divisions to produce four haploid spermatids. These differentiate into sperm. Sertoli cells provide support; interstitial cells release testosterone.

videos.title: Following sperm formation
videos.purpose: Identify where sperm develop and where maturation continues.
videos.fallback: Developing cells are found within seminiferous tubules. Their later stages approach the lumen. Sperm then enter the epididymis, where maturation develops the capacity for movement.

videos.title: Female reproductive anatomy
videos.purpose: Locate the ovary, oviduct, uterus, cervix and vagina.
videos.fallback: An oocyte is released from the ovary and guided toward the oviduct. Fertilization normally occurs in the oviduct. Implantation occurs later in the endometrium of the uterus.

videos.title: Coordinating the menstrual cycle
videos.purpose: Separate ovarian events from uterine events.
videos.fallback: Follicles develop and release estrogen before ovulation. After ovulation, the corpus luteum releases progesterone and some estrogen. Menstrual flow overlaps the early follicular phase of the next cycle.

videos.title: Hormonal control of the cycle
videos.purpose: Trace the estrogen rise, LH surge and later progesterone rise.
videos.fallback: Sustained high estrogen before ovulation promotes an LH surge. The surge helps trigger ovulation. The corpus luteum then releases progesterone; its later regression allows hormone support to fall.

videos.title: Hormonal contraception and feedback
videos.purpose: Connect an external hormone signal to altered pituitary stimulation.
videos.fallback: Combined hormonal methods provide estrogen and a progestin. Their feedback effects can limit FSH and LH stimulation and help prevent ovulation. They do not protect against STIs.

videos.title: Fertilization and the zygote — video support
videos.purpose: Explain where fertilization normally occurs, how one sperm contributes its chromosomes, and how the diploid chromosome number is restored.
videos.fallback: The sperm head has an acrosome containing enzymes that help it interact with and pass through the oocyte's surrounding layers. Reaching these layers is not yet the same as successfully fertilizing the cell. Membranes must interact and the sperm must contribute its contents. Fusion helps activate the oocyte. The oocyte completes meiosis II, and changes involving cortical granules modify the zona pellucida, the protective coat surrounding it. These changes help prevent additional sperm from entering. Do not imagine that many sperm are supposed to contribute chromosomes to one normal human zygote. The two chromosome contributions become associated with the developing cell's first division. For this chapter, focus on the result: one diploid cell containing genetic information from both gametes. The detailed chromosome movements will return in Chapter 16.

videos.title: Fetal development and developmental influences — video support
videos.purpose: Distinguish embryonic and fetal development, identify the age convention used, and explain how timing, dose and susceptibility affect developmental outcomes.
videos.fallback: During early development, the main body plan and basic organs become established. During the fetal period, these structures grow and mature. Brain development, skeletal changes and lung maturation continue; the appearance of an organ does not mean it is ready for independent function. Pregnancy is also divided into three trimesters. These are broad time groupings, not three abrupt biological switches. Early pregnancy emphasizes establishment of structures; the middle and later periods include substantial growth and functional maturation. A developmental timeline helps organize changes, but individual milestones vary. Do not use a single classroom diagram to predict an individual fetus's exact capacity to survive outside the uterus.

videos.title: Labour and birth as positive feedback — video support
videos.purpose: Trace cervical stretch, neural signalling and oxytocin, then distinguish the three stages of parturition.
videos.fallback: Stronger contractions can push the baby more firmly against the cervix, increasing stretch. That additional stretch promotes further signalling and oxytocin release. The response reinforces the initiating change instead of opposing it. This is why the loop is called positive feedback. The word positive does not mean “good.” It describes the relationship between response and stimulus. Compare negative feedback, in which a response reduces a deviation or decreases the signal that initiated it. Delivery removes much of the cervical-stretch stimulus from this particular loop. A feedback explanation is incomplete unless it identifies what ends or limits the amplification.

videos.title: Chromosomes, DNA and chromosome sets — video support
videos.purpose: Distinguish chromatin, chromosomes, homologous chromosomes and chromosome sets.
videos.fallback: A typical human body cell has 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs. Most pairs are homologous: the two chromosomes have the same genes at corresponding positions. One typically comes from the mother and one from the father. The alleles, or versions of those genes, need not be identical. The sex chromosomes require care. In an XX pair the chromosomes are homologous; X and Y share some corresponding regions but are not matching copies over their whole lengths. Autosomes are the chromosomes other than the sex chromosomes. A karyotype arranges photographed chromosomes by size and other features. videos.purpose: Use a homozygous recessive tester to distinguish possible parental genotypes and explain uncertainty from small samples.
videos.fallback: One aa offspring from B_ × bb means the dominant-phenotype parent must carry the recessive allele, assuming the model, parentage and observations are correct. It is heterozygous. For four independent offspring in an Aa × aa cross, the probability that all show the dominant phenotype is (1/2)⁴ = 1/16. videos.title: Recombination and sources of variation — video support
videos.purpose: Distinguish mutation, recombination and transfer of existing genetic material.
videos.fallback: Bacteria normally reproduce by binary fission, but they can also acquire DNA from other sources. Transformation involves uptake of external DNA. Conjugation involves direct contact and transfer, often including plasmids. Transduction involves a virus carrying bacterial genetic material. These mechanisms can introduce traits into a bacterial lineage. They are not the same as mitosis or the production and fusion of animal gametes. The important question is how the DNA enters and how it can persist in descendants. A transferred sequence must be maintained and expressed in an appropriate context to affect a phenotype. Detecting DNA outside a cell is not enough to establish a stable inherited change.

videos.title: Recombinant DNA and genetic engineering — video support
videos.purpose: Explain the conceptual roles of restriction enzymes, ligase, vectors and expression in recombinant-DNA technology.
videos.fallback: A transferred gene must be linked to appropriate expression signals and interpreted by the host machinery. Many human genes contain introns. Bacteria do not normally process human introns in the same way as human cells, so a suitable intron-free coding sequence may be used. Complementary DNA, or cDNA, can be made from a processed RNA template. This provides one route to an intron-free sequence. The conceptual point is that the host must receive usable coding information, not just any piece cut from a human chromosome. Production of a human protein in bacteria therefore depends on both the sequence and the expression context. The insulin example illustrates a biological manufacturing principle rather than a complete laboratory protocol.

videos.title: Populations, gene pools and genetic variation — video support
videos.purpose: Define a gene pool and distinguish change in a population from change within an individual.
videos.fallback: Microevolution is a change in allele frequencies across generations. An allele frequency is its share of all allele copies at the locus. It is a proportion, not simply the number of individuals showing a trait. Suppose a population doubles in size while every allele’s proportion stays the same. The number of copies increases, but the allele frequencies have not changed. Conversely, frequencies can change even if the total population size remains constant. An individual’s body can grow, develop or adjust to conditions. Those changes are not themselves evidence that a population’s inherited allele frequencies have changed.

videos.title: The Hardy–Weinberg model and its assumptions — video support
videos.purpose: Explain the model’s conditions and distinguish allele totals from expected genotype frequencies.
videos.fallback: The Hardy–Weinberg reference model assumes a very large population, random mating with respect to the locus, no mutation, no migration and no natural selection affecting the alleles or genotypes. A very large population minimizes chance fluctuations from sampling. Under these idealized conditions, allele frequencies remain constant across generations and genotype proportions follow p² + 2pq + q² = 1. The model gives a baseline for asking whether observed data fit the prediction. A real population need not satisfy every condition perfectly. A mismatch can suggest that assumptions need investigation, but the mismatch alone does not identify which mechanism caused it.

videos.title: Calculating expected genotype frequencies — video support
videos.purpose: Solve Hardy–Weinberg problems with explicit assumptions, separate quantities and reasonableness checks.
videos.fallback: Use the allele frequencies to calculate the expected genotype frequencies: p² = 0.36, 2pq = 0.48 and q² = 0.16. These are the expected fractions of AA, Aa and aa individuals. To obtain counts, multiply each frequency by N = 200. The expected numbers are 72 AA, 96 Aa and 32 aa. Check that the counts total 200 and the frequencies total 1. The heterozygotes are carriers in this simple recessive model. The dominant-phenotype fraction includes AA and Aa together, so it is 0.36 + 0.48 = 0.84, not p alone.

videos.title: Natural selection and non-random mating — video support
videos.purpose: Explain selection through differential reproductive success and distinguish it from mate-pairing effects.
videos.fallback: A trait can increase survival but reduce mating opportunities, or increase mating success while imposing a survival cost. Sexual selection focuses on differences in obtaining mates and reproducing. For example, a conspicuous display might attract mates while also increasing exposure to predators. The overall evolutionary effect depends on the balance of reproductive consequences, not on whether the display appears efficient to an observer. A claim that selection occurred needs evidence relating heritable differences to reproductive outcomes. A change in frequency alone can also arise through chance or movement between populations.

A claim that selection occurred needs evidence relating heritable differences to reproductive outcomes. A change in frequency alone can also arise through chance or movement between populations.

videos.title: Genetic drift, bottlenecks and founder effects — video support
videos.purpose: Distinguish chance sampling from selection and compare bottleneck and founder cases.
videos.fallback: A bottleneck occurs when population size falls sharply. The survivors may carry a smaller and unrepresentative sample of the earlier alleles. If the reduction is random with respect to a studied allele, drift can strongly change that allele’s frequency. If the population later increases, descendants reproduce the variation that survived. Recovery in numbers does not automatically bring back alleles that were lost. Mutation or gene flow might introduce variation later, but population growth alone does not guarantee restoration.

videos.title: Genetic diversity and conservation evidence — video support
videos.purpose: Use population-genetic mechanisms to evaluate conservation evidence without assuming a universal outcome.
videos.fallback: A connection between habitats may permit movement and gene flow. If migrants reproduce, new alleles can enter a population and genetic differentiation may decline. Whether this happens depends on actual movement, survival and reproduction. A population-management proposal should specify its biological mechanism and the evidence needed to evaluate it. Adding individuals, improving habitat and connecting populations are different interventions with potentially different effects. The effects can include trade-offs. For example, introduced individuals may carry genetic variants suited to a different environment. An evidence-based evaluation considers both genetic contribution and the ecological setting rather than assuming that every transfer is beneficial.

videos.title: Human populations and sharing the biosphere — video support
videos.purpose: Interpret demographic and resource-use evidence while distinguishing population size, per-person use and environmental effects.
videos.fallback: Total resource demand depends on both the number of people and the amount used per person, along with technology and the type of resource. A smaller population with high per-person use can have greater total demand for a particular resource than a larger population with lower use. For example, a hypothetical group of 1000 people using 3 units each demands 3000 units, while 2000 people using 1 unit each demand 2000 units. This simple accounting does not describe every environmental impact, but it shows why head count alone is insufficient. Resource extraction, waste and land-use change can affect habitat, species interactions and population connectivity. The mechanisms and measurements must be specified for the case.

videos.title: Life-history strategies and biotic potential — video support
videos.purpose: Compare life-history patterns as a continuum and interpret survivorship without treating categories as rigid rules.
videos.fallback: The r-associated end of a teaching continuum often includes early reproduction, many small offspring, short generation times and less investment in each offspring. Such traits can support rapid increase when conditions permit. The K-associated end often includes later reproduction, fewer offspring, longer lives and more investment per offspring. These are broad comparisons, not fixed laws that predict every trait or graph for every species. Some organisms combine features from both ends. Sea turtles, for example, produce many eggs yet can be long-lived as adults. Interpret the actual traits supplied rather than forcing every organism into a perfect category.

videos.purpose: Trace energy transfer and interpret predator–prey patterns without assuming correlation proves a single cause.
videos.fallback: When prey become more abundant, predators may have greater feeding success. Improved survival and reproduction can increase predator numbers after a delay. More predators can then contribute to increased prey mortality. A prey decline can later reduce predator reproduction or survival. Such feedback can contribute to oscillating patterns, but real populations are also affected by resources, disease, weather, migration and other interactions. Do not expect the peaks of both populations to occur at exactly the same time. A delay can arise because producing and raising offspring takes time.

videos.title: Mutualism, commensalism and parasitism — video support
videos.purpose: Use benefit, harm and no detected effect to classify close interspecific relationships.
videos.fallback: A mutualistic pollination case can provide food to a pollinator and transfer pollen for a plant. An epiphyte can gain physical support on a tree without taking nourishment from the tree; when no appreciable host effect is established, the model is commensalism. A parasite obtains resources from a host and imposes a cost. A tick feeding on a host is a familiar example. Parasites need not immediately kill the host, and the severity of harm varies. Name the resource or service and explain the effect on each partner. A label alone does not show that you understand the interaction.

videos.title: Primary and secondary succession — video support
videos.purpose: Distinguish primary and secondary succession and explain changing community composition without assuming one inevitable endpoint.
videos.fallback: Early colonizers can change a site by adding organic material, influencing soil conditions or altering light and moisture. Those changes can permit some later species and make conditions less suitable for others. Competition, dispersal and interactions also influence which populations establish. Not every later species is simply “better” than an earlier one; it may be favoured by different conditions. The community can become more structurally complex, but disturbance can interrupt or redirect the sequence. Local climate, available colonists and landform affect the pathway.
